summary.text: A swim bladder is a gas-filled organ inside bony fish that adjusts buoyancy, so a fish can hold a depth without constantly swimming.
It is related to the lungs of land vertebrates and lungfish, and it can also work as a chamber that produces or receives sound.
Some fish fill it by gulping air through a duct to the gut; in others that duct is lost and a gas gland adds the gas.

facts.label: Where it sits
facts.value: Normally two gas-filled sacs in the dorsal part

facts.label: Wall lining
facts.value: Guanine crystals make the walls impermeable to gases

facts.label: Fish without one
facts.value: Sharks and rays lack swim bladders

facts.label: Link to hearing
facts.value: Four Weberian ossicles join it to the inner ear

items.prompt: Unlike most sharks, a bony fish can hang motionless at a chosen depth without tiring. What lets it?

options.label: Oil-rich tissue that makes its whole body lighter
A heavier skeleton that sinks it to the right depth
Constant beating of its tail to stay level
An internal gas-filled organ whose volume it can adjust

items.explain: The swim bladder modulates buoyancy so the fish can stay at a desired depth without swimming, which would expend more energy.

items.prompt: A bony fish can drift at one depth, but most sharks that stop swimming sink. Why?

options.label: Most have no swim bladder, so only swimming gives them lift
Their skeletons are heavy bone that pulls them down
Their swim bladders are too small to hold gas
Their gills only work while the shark is moving

items.explain: Cartilaginous fish lack swim bladders, so most control depth by actively swimming, which produces dynamic lift.

items.prompt: Two fish are hauled upward fast from deep water. One's swim bladder still joins its gut by a duct; the other's does not. Which is in trouble?

options.label: The one with the duct, since air rushes in through it
The one with no duct, which cannot release gas and may burst
Both equally, since both fill only by gulping air
Neither, because the bladder adjusts instantly

items.explain: Physoclists, which lack the duct, cannot rise fast because the bladder would burst, while physostomes can burp out gas.

items.prompt: Boat sonar can pick out individual fish in dark water. What part of the fish gives the strong echo?

options.label: Its hard skull, which bounces sound straight back
Its scales, which act like a mirror to sound
The gas-filled bladder, where gas meets tissue
Its gills, which vibrate when sound hits them

items.explain: The gas/tissue interface at the swim bladder strongly reflects sound, which sonar equipment uses to find fish.

items.prompt: A deep sea eel keeps gas in its swim bladder at hundreds of bars of pressure. What makes that possible?

options.label: A gas gland acidifies the blood to free oxygen, and a countercurrent loop keeps it in
It swallows air at the surface and compresses it by diving
Its flexible walls squeeze the gas harder as it sinks
Guanine crystals pump gas inward through the walls

items.explain: The gas gland acidifies blood in the rete mirabile, freeing oxygen, and a countercurrent multiplication loop lets very high gas pressure build up.

items.prompt: In carp and catfish, the swim bladder helps with hearing. How is it connected to the ear?

options.label: A short duct carries air up to the ear
The gas gland sends sound along as bubbles
The guanine-lined wall touches the ear directly
A chain of four small bones carries vibrations to it

items.explain: In some mainly freshwater fish the bladder is linked to the inner ear by four Weberian ossicles, which carry vibrations and improve sound detection.
